questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a typical symptom of classic chronic Lyme encephalopathy?
questions.explanation: Lyme disease is caused by spirochaete Borrelia burgdorferi that is transmitted by Ixodes ticks. It has three stages: stage 1, rash; stage 2, early neurological signs, including lymphocytic meningitis, radicular pains, facial palsy, transverse myelitis and cranial and peripheral neuropathies; stage 3 (occurs 7 years after the initial diagnosis), late neurological signs, including Bell’s palsy, dementia, encephalomyelitis, hemianopsia, hemiplegia, radiculo-neuropathy and seizures. Other typical symptoms of chronic Lyme encephalopathy include poor memory and concentration, fatigue, daytime hypersomnolence, irritability and depression. References: Levenson JL (2004). The American Psychiatric Publishing Textbook of Psychosomatic Medicine. Arlington, VA: American Psychiatric Publishing, p. 583; Puri BK, Hall AD, Ho RC (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. Boca Raton, FL: CRC Press, pp. 502–503.

questions.question_text: What is the estimated incidence of developing Ebstein anomaly if the mother is exposed to lithium in the first trimester?
questions.explanation: The incidence has been estimated to be between 0.05% and 0.1% after maternal exposure to lithium in the first trimester. Reference: Puri BK, Hall AD, Ho RC (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. Boca Raton, FL: CRC Press, p. 561.

questions.question_text: If a mother with bipolar disorder is maintained on sodium valproate throughout pregnancy, what is the estimated incidence of neural tube defects?
questions.explanation: The incidence of foetal birth defect (mainly neural tube defect) has been estimated to be around 1 in 100. Reference: Puri BK, Hall AD, Ho RC (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. Boca Raton, FL: CRC Press, p. 561.

questions.question_text: Which particular chromosomal loci have been implicated with autistic disorder?
questions.explanation: The heritability of the disorder has been found to be over 90%. The recurrence rate in siblings is roughly 3% for narrowly defined autism but is around 10%–20% for milder variants. The loci may involve chromosomes 2q and 7q. Family history of schizophrenia-like psychosis or affective disorder has been implicated as well. Reference: Puri BK, Hall AD, Ho RC (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. Boca Raton, FL: CRC Press, p. 623.

questions.question_text: An 18-year-old female has been referred by her school counsellor, as he was concerned that she might have depression. In adolescent-onset bipolar disorder, which of the following symptoms is less likely to occur compared with adult-onset depression?
questions.explanation: The mean duration of a depressive episode in children is around 7–9 months. The symptoms are similar to that of adults with a minimum of 2 weeks period of sadness, irritability, loss of interest and loss of pleasure. There is usually also impairment in social and role functions. Anxiety symptoms and conduct disorders are commonly associated. It should be noted that children tend to have lesser psychomotor retardation in comparison with adults. Reference: Puri BK, Hall AD, Ho RC (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. Boca Raton, FL: CRC Press, p. 648.

questions.question_text: Psychotherapy is one of the core modalities for the treatment of individuals with borderline personality disorder. Which of the following therapies targets mainly the distorted perceptions of significant others?
questions.explanation: In transference-focused therapy, it aims at correcting distorted perceptions of significant others and decreasing symptoms and self-destructive behaviours. Reference: Puri BK, Hall AD, Ho RC (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. Boca Raton, FL: CRC Press, p. 446.

questions.question_text: A 32-year-woman has always had difficulties with trusting others. She also does not feel that her spouse has been faithful towards her. She has been referred and seen by the outpatient psychiatry team, who has diagnosed her with paranoid personality disorder. Which of the following treatments is least likely to be suitable for her?
questions.explanation: Supportive therapy and problem-solving therapy are indicated for her. Cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT) is also helpful for her condition. Cognitive therapy would help to target the core beliefs, such as how others are malicious and deceptive. In behaviour therapy, the patient is involved in role play to handle hostility and personal attacks in daily life. A course of antidepressant is also likely to be helpful. Reference: Puri BK, Hall AD, Ho RC (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. Boca Raton, FL: CRC Press, p. 443.

questions.question_text: A 50-year-old man with a history of cardiac arrhythmia and a pacemaker implant has been admitted to the NHS service following a severe bout of depression with strong suicidal ideations. All the following are relative contraindications against electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) with the exception of
questions.explanation: Studies have demonstrated that, with proper pre-electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) cardiac and pacemaker/defibrillator assessment, ECT can be safely and effectively administered to patients with an implanted cardiac device. Reference: Dolenc TJ et al. (2004). Electroconvulsive therapy in patients with cardiac pacemakers and implantable cardioverter defibrillators. Pacing Clin Electrophysiol, 27(9): 1257–1263.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is false about the findings from the Multimodal Treatment Study (MTA) on attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)?

options.text: There is a small but detectible reduction in overall growth in height for children who remain on stimulants.
Loss of growth is maximal in the first year of treatment.
35% showed a moderate and gradual improvement, and 50% showed significant improvement over the 3-year study period.
15% initially responded well but deteriorated over 3 years.
Drug treatment was associated with a reduction in the rate of delinquency and substance abuse in children with ADHD, compared to the rate found in normal controls.

correct_answer.text: Drug treatment was associated with a reduction in the rate of delinquency and substance abuse in children with ADHD, compared to the rate found in normal controls.

correct_answers.text: Drug treatment was associated with a reduction in the rate of delinquency and substance abuse in children with ADHD, compared to the rate found in normal controls.

questions.explanation: The MTA study shows that children with ADHD continue to show higher than normal rates of delinquency (four times) and substance use (two times). In the MTA study, 485 children took part in the 3-year follow-up. The mean age was 12 years. Primary outcomes were ADHD and oppositional defiant disorder symptoms, reading scores, social skills, level of impairment and diagnosis. After year 1, the research protocol was dropped, allowing more naturalistic and personalized treatment. Reference: Bates G (2009). Drug treatments for attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder in young people. Adv Psych Treat, 15: 162–171.

questions.question_text: The male-to-female ratio in hypothyroidism is
questions.explanation: This is a condition that affects 2%–5% of women, mostly between ages 20 and 45 years, with a female-to-male ratio of 5:1. Reference: Puri BK, Treasaden I (eds) (2010). Psychiatry: An Evidence-Based Text. Hodder Arnold, pp. 576–577.

questions.question_text: A 65-year-old woman has been having difficulties with her sleep. Which of the following are not characteristic sleep changes that take place in aging?
questions.explanation: Sleep parameters that increase in old age include sleep latency, frequency of awakenings, episodes and fragmentation of REM sleep. Parameters that decrease include duration of slow-wave sleep, sleep efficiency and total sleep time. Reference: Puri BK, Hall AD, Ho RC (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. Boca Raton, FL: CRC Press, p. 679.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a feature of non-REM sleep?
questions.explanation: Non-REM sleep occurs when there is reduced neuronal activity. Features include decreased complexity of dreams, increased parasympathetic activity, abolition of tendon reflexes, decreased heart rate, decreased systolic blood pressure, decreased respiratory rate, decreased cerebral blood flow and, usually, no penile erection. Reference: Puri BK, Hall AD, Ho RC (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. Boca Raton, FL: CRC Press, p. 216.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is false?

options.text: After treatment of hyperthyroidism, psychiatric symptoms usually resolve.
One-third of patients with hyperthyroidism meet the criteria for major depressive disorder.
Delusions and hallucinations are equally common in hypothyroidism.

questions.explanation: Hypothyroidism is associated with hair loss, not hirsutism. Reference: Puri BK, Treasaden I (eds) (2010). Psychiatry: An Evidence-Based Text. Hodder Arnold, pp. 576–577.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not considered to be subcortical dementia?
questions.explanation: Typical examples of cortical dementia include Alzheimer dementia, frontal-lobe dementia and CJD. Examples of subcortical dementia include HIV-related dementia, Huntington chorea and Parkinson disease. Mixed cortical and subcortical dementia include vascular dementia and dementia with Lewy bodies. Reference: Puri BK, Hall AD, Ho RC (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. Boca Raton, FL: CRC Press, p. 693.

questions.question_text: Which of the following neuroanatomical areas shows decreased blood flow during the Wisconsin Card Sorting Test (WCST) in patients with schizophrenia?
questions.explanation: People with schizophrenia performing the WCST, which normally activates the frontal lobe, have decreased blood flow in the frontal cortex. Hypofrontality is associated with negative symptoms of schizophrenia. Reference: Puri BK, Hall AD, Ho RC (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. Boca Raton, FL: CRC Press, p. 363.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements regarding the standard error of the mean (SEM) is false?

options.text: It decreases as the sample size increases.
It increases as the standard deviation increases.
It is a measure of the variability of the observations.
It measures the variability of the sample statistic in relation to the true but unknown population characteristic.

correct_answer.text: It is a measure of the variability of the observations.

correct_answers.text: It is a measure of the variability of the observations.

questions.explanation: The SEM is the SD of the sample mean’s estimate of a population mean. It describes the uncertainty of how the sample mean represents the population mean. The SD describes variability between individuals. As SEM is always less than SD, it misleads readers into underestimating individual variability. Reference: Nagele P (2003). Misuse of standard error of the mean (SEM) when reporting variability of a sample. Br J Anaesth, 90(4): 514–516.

questions.question_text: Twenty depressed patients were given escitalopram and matched with another 20 depressed patients, who were given agomelatine. The Montgomery–Asberg Depression Rating Scale was used to assess these patients’ response to the medication. Which of the following tests below can be used to compare treatment effect?
questions.explanation: The independent sample t-test is used to compare means of two independent groups. It assumes differences between groups are normally distributed. It is commonly used in case–control trials and matched-pair randomized controlled trials. Reference: Everitt BS (2006). Medical Statistics from A to Z (2nd edition). Cambridge University Press, pp. 225–226.

questions.question_text: Referring to Figure 5.1, intention to treat analysis was used. How many participants should be included?
questions.explanation: Intention to treat (ITT) analysis includes all patients randomised. Those lost to follow-up or who discontinue are included as treatment failures or by last observation carried forward. As a result, 26 participants who consented and were randomised are included in the final analysis. Excluding dropouts would overestimate treatment effect.

questions.question_text: Based on Table 5.1, calculate the rate of depressed subjects with intervention.
questions.explanation: Depressed subjects / Total in intervention = 28 / 59 = 0.47. This is the experimental event rate (EER).

questions.question_text: Based on Table 5.1, calculate the rate of depressed subjects with the control group?
questions.explanation: Depressed subjects / Total in control = 36 / 57 = 0.63. This is the control event rate (CER).

questions.question_text: Based on Table 5.1, what is the absolute benefit increase?
questions.explanation: Absolute benefit increase = EER – CER = 0.63 – 0.47 = 0.16.

questions.question_text: Based on Table 5.1, what is the relative risk of remaining depressed?
questions.explanation: Relative risk = EER / CER = 0.63 / 0.47 = 1.34.

questions.question_text: Based on Table 5.1, what is the relative benefit increase?
questions.explanation: Relative benefit increase = (EER – CER) / CER = (0.63 – 0.47) / 0.47 = 0.34.

questions.question_text: Based on Table 5.1, what is the number needed to treat (NNT)?
questions.explanation: NNT = 1 / |ARR| = 1 / 0.16 = 6.25 ≈ 6 patients.

questions.question_text: If the confidence interval (CI) of absolute risk reduction (ARR) is 0.16 (95% CI: 0.04–0.35), what is the CI of NNT?
questions.explanation: Lower limit of CI for NNT = 1 / 0.35 = 2.86; upper limit = 1 / 0.04 = 25.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a sign of inhalant intoxication?
questions.explanation: Inhalant intoxication leads to depressed reflexes (hyporeflexia) rather than hyper-reflexia, since inhalants act as central nervous system depressants. Other signs include giddiness, poor coordination, unsteady gait, nystagmus, diplopia, lethargy, tremors, generalized muscle weakness, euphoria, psychomotor slowing and stupor or coma. Reference: Sadock BJ, Sadock VA (2003). Kaplan and Sadock’s Synopsis of Psychiatry (9th edition). Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, pp. 441–442; Garland EL, Howard MO (2014). Adverse consequences of acute inhalant intoxication. Exp Clin Psychopharmacol, 19(2): 134–144.

questions.question_text: A 64-year-old man with Parkinson disease is noted by the family to persistently gamble in the casino, despite having lost huge sums of money and being in debt. Premorbidly, he only gambled small amounts sparingly. Which one of the following drugs that he was taking could potentially cause pathological gambling?
questions.explanation: Pathological gambling is a rare potential complication of Parkinson disease treatment. A study by Dodd et al. (2005) found that dopamine agonist therapy, especially pramipexole, was associated with potentially reversible pathological gambling, likely due to disproportionate stimulation of dopamine D3 receptors in the limbic system. Reference: Dodd ML, Klos KJ et al. (2005). Pathological gambling caused by drugs used to treat Parkinson disease. Arch Neurol, 62: 1377–1381.

questions.question_text: Which of the following offences or misconduct are not more predominantly committed by male offenders?
questions.explanation: Most serious offences including murder, manslaughter, robbery with violence, sexual aggression and homosexual offences are predominantly committed by males. Threat and fraud are committed relatively more frequently by females than these other offences. Reference: Chiswick D, Cope R (1995). Seminars in Forensic Psychiatry. Gaskell.

questions.question_text: A 37-year-old male sex offender is being assessed for risk of recidivism. Which of the following is the best predictor of sexual reoffending?
questions.explanation: A meta-analysis of 82 recidivism studies identified antisocial orientation and deviant sexual preferences as the major predictors of sexual recidivism. The other listed factors have little or no predictive value. Reference: Hanson RK, Morton-Bourgon KE (2005). The characteristics of persistent sexual offenders: A meta-analysis of recidivism studies. J Consult Clin Psychol, 73: 1154–1163.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is false regarding tuberous sclerosis?

options.text: Approximately two-thirds of all cases are spontaneous mutations, while one-third are inherited on an autosomal dominant basis.
It is associated with mental retardation in approximately half of patients.
It is associated with cardiac rhabdomyomas and pulmonary cysts.
Progression of adult-onset cases tends to be much faster than childhood-onset cases.

correct_answer.text: Progression of adult-onset cases tends to be much faster than childhood-onset cases.

correct_answers.text: Progression of adult-onset cases tends to be much faster than childhood-onset cases.

questions.explanation: In adult-onset cases, progression tends to be much slower than in childhood-onset cases, and adults may have a normal lifespan. Early-onset cases often have severe epilepsy and rarely survive more than 15 years. Reference: Moore DP, Puri BK (2012). Textbook of Clinical Neuropsychiatry and Behavioral Neuroscience (3rd edition). Hodder Arnold, pp. 456–457.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is false regarding foetal alcohol syndrome?

options.text: Binge alcohol drinking in pregnant mothers may be as dangerous as daily drinking in this syndrome.
It is associated with mental retardation, which, in most cases, is of mild severity.
It is associated with behavioural problems similar to those of ADHD, but hyperactivity is more prominent than distractibility and inattentiveness.
It is caused by in utero exposure to alcohol.
There is often some resolution of the dysmorphic features by adulthood.

correct_answer.text: It is associated with behavioural problems similar to those of ADHD, but hyperactivity is more prominent than distractibility and inattentiveness.

correct_answers.text: It is associated with behavioural problems similar to those of ADHD, but hyperactivity is more prominent than distractibility and inattentiveness.

questions.explanation: Foetal alcohol syndrome is related to maternal alcohol ingestion; binge drinking may be as dangerous as daily drinking. It is associated with mild mental retardation, behavioural problems similar to ADHD, though distractibility and inattentiveness are more prominent than hyperactivity. Dysmorphic features often partially resolve by adulthood. Reference: Moore DP, Puri BK (2012). Textbook of Clinical Neuropsychiatry and Behavioral Neuroscience (3rd edition). Hodder Arnold, p. 466.

questions.question_text: A morbidly obese 13-year-old boy has difficulty controlling his overeating. He often goes to extreme lengths to satisfy his hunger. He also tends to prick his skin and gets irritable easily. He attends a special school because of a diagnosis of mild learning disability when he was younger. On physical examination, he is short in stature and has micropenis with cryptorchidism. Which one of the following diagnoses is most likely?
questions.explanation: Prader–Willi syndrome is characterized by extreme hyperphagia, obesity, mild mental retardation and dysmorphic features. Patients may have behavioural problems including skin pricking, ritualized behaviour and temper tantrums. Hypogonadism presents as micropenis and cryptorchidism in males. Reference: Moore DP, Puri BK (2012). Textbook of Clinical Neuropsychiatry and Behavioral Neuroscience (3rd edition). Hodder Arnold, p. 465.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a risk factor for suicide in patients with schizophrenia?

options.text: Discharge from inpatient care 3 months and beyond
Having low educational attainment before onset of the illness

questions.explanation: About 10% of patients with schizophrenia commit suicide, often early in the illness. Risk factors include being male, young, unemployed; having chronic illness with relapses; high educational attainment; akathisia; abruptly stopping medication; and recent discharge from inpatient care. Regaining insight into illness can precipitate depression and suicidal risk. Reference: Puri BK, Hall AD, Ho RC (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. Boca Raton, FL: CRC Press, p. 371.

questions.question_text: Risk of future antisocial personality disorder in a 14-year-old child with conduct disorder is
questions.explanation: Forty percent of young people with conduct disorder develop antisocial (dissocial) personality disorder in adulthood. Predictors include borderline IQ, mental retardation and family history of dissocial personality disorder. Reference: Puri BK, Hall AD, Ho RC (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. Boca Raton, FL: CRC Press, p. 635.

questions.question_text: Which of the following disorders is recognized to cause schizophrenia-like psychosis in a 40-year-old man?

options.text: Cerebral autosomal-dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy (CADASIL)
Mitochondrial encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes (MELAS) syndrome
Polyneuropathy, organomegaly, endocrinopathy, monoclonal gammopathy and skin changes (POEMS) syndrome

questions.explanation: Huntington disease is a dominantly inherited, neurodegenerative disorder due to expansion of a trinucleotide repeat in chromosome 4. It presents with choreic movements, cognitive decline and psychiatric symptoms. Paranoid schizophrenia-like symptoms occur in 6%–25% of cases. Reference: Correa BB et al. (2006). Association of Huntington’s disease and schizophrenia-like psychosis in a Huntington’s disease pedigree. Clin Pract Epidemiol Ment Health, 2(1): 1.

questions.question_text: A 22-year-old university student suffers from first episode psychosis and has great difficulty with her studies. She was diagnosed to have schizophrenia. Which of the following neurocognitive functions is most impaired?
questions.explanation: A meta-analysis found that neurocognitive deficits are most marked in immediate verbal memory and processing speed in first-episode schizophrenia. Reference: Mesholam-Gately RI et al. (2009). Neurocognition in first-episode schizophrenia: A meta-analytic review. Neuropsychology, 23(3): 315–336.

questions.question_text: Nicotine causes addiction through its action as which of the following?
questions.explanation: Nicotine produces positive reinforcing and addictive effects by activating the dopaminergic pathway from the ventral tegmental area to the cerebral cortex and limbic system. It also increases circulating noradrenaline and adrenaline and the release of vasopressin, beta-endorphin, ACTH and cortisol. Reference: Sadock BJ, Sadock VA (2003). Kaplan and Sadock’s Synopsis of Psychiatry (9th edition). Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, p. 445.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a general principle behind motivational interviewing?
questions.explanation: Psychoeducation is not one of the core principles of motivational interviewing. The key principles are express empathy, develop discrepancy, roll with resistance and support self-efficacy. Reference: Miller WR et al. (1992). Motivational Enhancement Therapy Manual. National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism, pp. 13–35.

questions.question_text: A 49-year-old male offender with a history of schizophrenia is released from a medium-secure unit. What is the probability that he will reoffend within 2 years?
questions.explanation: Studies in England and Wales show that patients discharged from medium-secure units reoffend within 2 years at rates of about 16% for men and 9% for women. A national cohort study found male reconviction around 10%. Reference: Maden A et al. (2006). Gender differences in reoffending after discharge from medium-secure units. Br J Psychiatry, 189: 168–172.

questions.question_text: What percentage of perpetrators of homicide have symptoms of mental illness at the time of the offence?
questions.explanation: The National Confidential Inquiry into Suicide and Homicide by People with Mental Illness found that among 1,594 convicted of homicide, 10% had symptoms of mental illness at the time of offence, 34% had a lifetime history of mental illness, and 5% had schizophrenia. Reference: Shaw J et al. (2006). Rates of mental disorder in people convicted of homicide. Br J Psychiatry, 188: 143–147.

questions.question_text: A newborn child with Down syndrome is found on genetic testing to have an unbalanced Robertsonian translocation, and you are asked to counsel the parents. Which one of the following pieces of advice is incorrect?

options.text: Both parents should be offered chromosome analysis, as one may carry the translocation in a balanced form.
If the mother is found to be a carrier, the recurrence risk is 50%.
Ultrasound monitoring of nasal bone formation will be useful in future antenatal screening for Down syndrome.
If parents are carriers of translocation, they have 46 chromosomes.
In translocation, patients with Down syndrome have 46 chromosomes.

correct_answer.text: If the mother is found to be a carrier, the recurrence risk is 50%.

correct_answers.text: If the mother is found to be a carrier, the recurrence risk is 50%.

questions.explanation: The recurrence risk for a carrier of a Robertsonian translocation is approximately 10%–15%, not 50%. Ninety-four percent of Down syndrome cases are due to meiotic nondisjunction (47 chromosomes), 5% to translocations (46 chromosomes), and 1% to mosaicism. Reference: Puri BK, Hall AD, Ho RC (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. Boca Raton, FL: CRC Press, p. 661.

questions.question_text: Hachinski score is indicated for which particular form of dementia?
questions.explanation: The Hachinski Ischemic Score helps distinguish vascular dementia (score > 7) from Alzheimer’s dementia (score < 4) by assessing course, symptoms, history and focal neurological findings. Reference: Puri BK, Hall AD, Ho RC (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. Boca Raton, FL: CRC Press, p. 700.

questions.question_text: Based on your understanding of Lewy body dementia (LBD), how common is the presence of visual hallucinations?
questions.explanation: Complex visual hallucinations occur in 80% of individuals with Lewy body dementia, while auditory hallucinations occur in 20%. Eighty percent experience visual hallucinations and 65% have delusions. Reference: Puri BK, Hall AD, Ho RC (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. Boca Raton, FL: CRC Press, p. 702.

questions.question_text: In Figure 5.2, cluster 1 has more cases of depressive disorder, adjustment, stress, panic attack, first suicide attempt and no admissions. Cluster 2 has more cases of borderline personality disorder, hallucination, insomnia, headache, multiple attempts and multiple admissions. Which of the clustering algorithms was used to generate Figure 5.2?
questions.explanation: The study used connectivity-based clustering, which forms clusters by linking similar cases based on connections. Centroid-based uses central vectors, density-based uses data density, and distribution-based uses statistical distributions – none apply here. Reference: Choo C et al. (2014). Cluster analysis reveals risk factors for repeated suicide attempts. Asian J Psychiatr, 8: 38–51.

questions.question_text: Referring to Figure 5.3, which of the following should be the x-axis?
questions.explanation: A receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve plots sensitivity versus (1 – specificity). Therefore the x-axis is 1 – specificity. Reference: Mak A et al. (2011). Damage accrual, cumulative glucocorticoid dose and depression predict anxiety in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus. Clin Rheumatol, 30(6): 795–803.

questions.question_text: The cut-off score of an anxiety inventory is 40. If the sensitivity and specificity of this inventory for diagnosing anxiety are 0.42 and 0.95, respectively, what is the likelihood ratio for a positive test result (LR+)?
questions.explanation: LR+ = sensitivity / (1 – specificity) = 0.42 / (1 – 0.95) = 0.42 / 0.05 = 8.4. A high LR+ far from 1 indicates strong evidence for disease when the test is positive.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is false about type II error?

options.text: The null hypothesis is wrongly rejected.
The study does not detect an effect that existed in reality.
Type II errors are considered to be less serious than type I error.
Type II errors occur when the sample size of a study is too small.
Type II errors represent false negatives.

correct_answer.text: The null hypothesis is wrongly rejected.

correct_answers.text: The null hypothesis is wrongly rejected.

questions.explanation: Type II error occurs when the null hypothesis is not rejected when it should be (false negative). It does not detect a real effect. Type II errors are usually considered less serious than type I errors. Restricting type I error by a low alpha increases type II error risk. Reference: Lewis GH et al. (2008). Mastering Public Health. Royal Society of Medicine Press, pp. 87–88.

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old man has been using cannabis for a year. He experiences withdrawal effects if he misses his regular dose. He is now keen to quit his habit. Which of the following medications would be helpful in treating his cannabis dependence syndrome?
questions.explanation: No medications have been consistently effective or approved; treatments studied include agents for withdrawal symptoms or affecting cannabinoid receptors. Busprione is the only medication to show efficacy for cannabis dependence in a controlled clinical trial. Reference: Weinstein AM et al. (2011). Pharmacological treatment of cannabis dependence. Curr Pharm Des, 17(4): 1351–1358.

questions.question_text: A 15-year-old boy is convicted of rape and undergoes treatment for sexual offenders. Which one of the following statements is most accurate about his recidivism rate compared with that of a 30-year-old man?

options.text: A 15-year-old has a higher rate of recidivism for sexual offence compared with a 30-year-old.
A 15-year-old has a lower rate of recidivism for sexual offence compared with a 30-year-old.
A 15-year-old has a higher rate of recidivism for non-sexual offence compared with the 30-year-old.
A 15-year-old has a lower rate of recidivism for non-sexual offence compared with a 30-year-old.
Their risk of recidivism for sexual offences is similar.

correct_answer.text: A 15-year-old has a lower rate of recidivism for sexual offence compared with a 30-year-old.

correct_answers.text: A 15-year-old has a lower rate of recidivism for sexual offence compared with a 30-year-old.

questions.explanation: Adolescent sex offenders show lower sexual recidivism rates than adults when given treatment. Studies report adolescent sexual recidivism rates of 5%–14%, indicating better treatment response and lower repeat offending compared with 30-year-olds. Reference: National Centre on Sexual Behaviour of Youth (2003). NCSBY Fact Sheet.

questions.question_text: Which of the following antibiotics can cause euphoria, delusions, depersonalization and illusions?
questions.explanation: Cephalosporins can cause euphoria, delusions, depersonalization and illusions. Antibiotic psychiatric toxicity may result from GABA antagonism, pyridoxine deficiency, alcohol interactions or protein synthesis inhibition. Clarithromycin is associated with delirium and mania; gentamicin and TMP-SMX with delirium and psychosis; quinolones with psychosis, paranoia, mania, agitation and Tourette-like syndrome. References: Levenson JL. The American Psychiatric Publishing Textbook of Psychosomatic Medicine. Sternbach H, State R (1997). Antibiotics: Neuropsychiatric effects. Harv Rev Psychiatry, 5(4): 214–226.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about cannabis and schizophrenia is not true?

options.text: Cannabis has been known to lead to a twofold increase in the risk of schizophrenia.
Cannabis has been known to lead to a fourfold increase in the risk of psychosis.
Not all cannabis users develop schizophrenia, and this is dependent on the catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT) genotype.
Patients who have homozygous VAL/VAL alleles in the COMT genotype have relatively higher risk.
Patients who are homozygous for MET/MET alleles in the COMT genotype have a twofold higher risk.

correct_answer.text: Patients who are homozygous for MET/MET alleles in the COMT genotype have a twofold higher risk.

correct_answers.text: Patients who are homozygous for MET/MET alleles in the COMT genotype have a twofold higher risk.

questions.explanation: Studies show individuals with VAL/VAL alleles in the COMT genotype have higher schizophrenia risk with cannabis, whereas MET/MET homozygotes have no increased risk. Cannabis increases psychosis risk fourfold but schizophrenia risk twofold. Reference: Puri BK, Hall AD, Ho RC (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. Boca Raton, FL: CRC Press, p. 361.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a good prognostic factor for patients with schizophrenia?

options.text: Abrupt or late onset of the illness

questions.explanation: Good prognostic factors include female gender, being married, good premorbid adjustment, family history of affective disorder, short illness duration before treatment, absence of ventricular enlargement and abrupt or late onset. Being male is not a good prognostic factor. Reference: Puri BK, Hall AD, Ho RC (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. Boca Raton, FL: CRC Press, p. 370.

questions.question_text: The STAR*D trial’s main purpose is to determine the effectiveness of different treatments for major depressive disorder patients unresponsive to an initial antidepressant. In Level 2 of the trial, which one of the following is not a treatment strategy used?

options.text: Switching to other antidepressants from the SSRI class (sertraline)

questions.explanation: Level 2 strategies include (1) switching to another antidepressant (sertraline, venlafaxine, bupropion) and/or cognitive therapy, (2) medication and psychotherapy augmentation, (3) antidepressant-only switch, (4) antidepressant-only augmentation, (5) psychotherapy-only switch, and (6) psychotherapy-only augmentation. Augmentation with physical therapies was not used. Reference: Puri BK, Hall AD, Ho RC (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. Boca Raton, FL: CRC Press, p. 392.

questions.question_text: A 28-year-old man presents with tall stature, small penis and small testes, low libido and erectile dysfunction, low testosterone and elevated FSH, and no family history. Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Klinefelter syndrome is due to one or more extra X chromosomes. Characterized by tall stature, hypogonadism and infertility, often diagnosed during infertility or erectile dysfunction workup. Reference: Moore DP, Puri BK (2012). Textbook of Clinical Neuropsychiatry and Behavioral Neuroscience (3rd edition). Hodder Arnold, p. 460.

questions.question_text: In the United Kingdom, which of the following occupations is associated with the highest rate of suicide?
questions.explanation: A meta-analysis of 34 studies found elementary professionals had the highest suicide rates, followed by machine operators and deck crew, then agricultural workers. Reference: Allison Milner et al. (2013). Suicide by occupation: systematic review and meta-analysis. Br J Psychiatry, 203: 409–416.

questions.question_text: Generally, the outcome for bulimia nervosa improves over time and is better than that of anorexia nervosa. In terms of long-term outcomes, which psychiatric condition is highly associated with bulimia nervosa?
questions.explanation: About 50% of bulimia nervosa patients recover or have moderate eating attitude abnormalities after 10 years. Depression is highly comorbid and is a negative prognostic factor, with prominent anorectic features worsening response. Reference: Puri BK, Hall AD, Ho RC (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. Boca Raton, FL: CRC Press, p. 587.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is false regarding the correlation coefficient?

options.text: The correlation coefficient can be strong but statistically non-significant because of sample size.
Spearman’s and Kendall’s rank correlation coefficients are non-parametric alternatives to Pearson’s correlation coefficient.
The value of a correlation coefficient can range from −1 to +1.
A value of 0.5–0.8 signifies strong correlation.

correct_answer.text: A value of 0.5–0.8 signifies strong correlation.

correct_answers.text: A value of 0.5–0.8 signifies strong correlation.

questions.explanation: The correlation coefficient (r) ranges from −1 to +1. Strength is interpreted as 0–0.2 negligible, 0.2–0.5 weak, 0.5–0.8 moderate, 0.8–1.0 strong. Thus 0.5–0.8 is moderate, not strong. Reference: Everitt BS (2006). Medical Statistics from A to Z (2nd edition). Cambridge University Press, p. 60.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following statements is true regarding type II error?

options.text: It can lead to false negatives.
The null hypothesis was wrongly rejected.
Study shows an effect that in reality does not exist.
The more the study restricts type I errors by setting a low level of alpha, the less the chance that a type II error will occur.
Type II errors are generally considered to be more serious than type I errors.

correct_answer.text: It can lead to false negatives.

correct_answers.text: It can lead to false negatives.

questions.explanation: Type II error occurs when the null hypothesis is not rejected when it should be, resulting in false negatives. Restricting type I error by a low alpha increases the chance of type II error. Type II errors are generally considered less serious than type I errors. Reference: Lewis GH et al. (2008). Mastering Public Health. Royal Society of Medicine Press, pp. 87–88.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about type I error is false?

options.text: Bonferroni correction can be used to keep type II errors at a low level.
The null hypothesis is wrongly rejected.
The study shows an effect that does not exist.
The more the study restricts type I errors by setting a low level of alpha, the greater the chance that a type II error will occur.
Type I errors are more serious than type II errors.

correct_answer.text: Bonferroni correction can be used to keep type II errors at a low level.

correct_answers.text: Bonferroni correction can be used to keep type II errors at a low level.

questions.explanation: Bonferroni correction is used to control type I error rate when multiple comparisons are performed, not type II errors. Type I error is false-positive (rejecting the true null hypothesis). Restricting type I error by low alpha increases type II error risk. Reference: Everitt BS (2006). Medical Statistics from A to Z (2nd edition). Cambridge University Press, p. 238; Lewis GH et al. (2008). Mastering Public Health. Royal Society of Medicine Press.

questions.question_text: Approximately, what percentage of patients with schizophrenia are non-concordant with their medications?
questions.explanation: Between 40% and 60% of patients with schizophrenia are non-concordant with oral medications. Reasons include limited insight, limited perceived benefit, adverse effects, external pressure and poor therapeutic engagement. Reference: Puri BK, Hall AD, Ho RC (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. Boca Raton, FL: CRC Press, p. 365.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is true about exhibitionism?

options.text: Exhibitionism is commonly associated with homosexual behaviour.
Exhibitionism is commonly associated with exposure of the genitalia to an unsuspecting stranger of the opposite gender.
Exhibitionism is commonly associated with sexual assault.
Exhibitionism is commonly associated with voyeurism.
Exhibitionism is commonly associated with young men.

correct_answer.text: Exhibitionism is commonly associated with exposure of the genitalia to an unsuspecting stranger of the opposite gender.

correct_answers.text: Exhibitionism is commonly associated with exposure of the genitalia to an unsuspecting stranger of the opposite gender.

questions.explanation: Exhibitionism describes the continual or repetitive desire to expose one’s genitals to strangers, usually of the opposite sex, without seeking or desiring any further contact. Reference: Puri BK, Treasaden I (eds) (2010). Psychiatry: An Evidence-Based Text. London: Hodder Arnold, pp. 749, 762, 766–767.

questions.question_text: Which of the following medications is likely to be helpful for patients with agoraphobia as well as social phobia?
questions.explanation: Selective serotonin re-uptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are usually the first-line treatments for phobic anxiety disorder. MAOIs are effective for patients with social phobia and agoraphobia. Of note, 80%–90% of pure social phobic are almost asymptomatic at week 16, based on a previous research. Reference: Puri BK, Hall AD, Ho RC (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. Boca Raton, FL: CRC Press, p. 407.

questions.question_text: A 20-year-old man has been diagnosed with kleptomania. All the following are possible comorbid psychiatric disorders that a psychiatrist should assess for, with the exception of which of the following?
questions.explanation: Kleptomania is an impulse-control disorder characterized by repeated failure to resist the impulse to steal, in which tension is then relieved by stealing. The sex ratio of female to male is 4:1. Pure kleptomania is extremely rare. The treating psychiatrist should look out for other psychiatric disorders, such as depression, anxiety, bulimia nervosa, sexual dysfunction as well as fetishistic disorder. Reference: Puri BK, Hall AD, Ho RC (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. Boca Raton, FL: CRC Press, p. 724.

questions.question_text: Which of the following biases could be minimized by blinding in a randomized controlled trial?
questions.explanation: Measurement bias results in errors that occur in instruments and inaccuracies or incompleteness of data collection, which affects the groups to differing degrees. There are three types of measurement bias: instrument bias, recall bias and observer bias. Blinding of participants avoids respondent bias, blinding of practitioners who are treating study participants avoids instrument bias and blinding of the observer who collects measurements or analyses results avoids observer bias. Reference: Lewis GH, Sheringham J, Kalim K, Crayford TJB (2008). Mastering Public Health: A Postgraduate Guide to Examination and Revalidation. London: Royal Society of Medicine Press, pp. 27–30.

questions.question_text: A researcher wants to compare the responses (graded as mild, moderate and high responses) of a group of depressed patients on bupropion, with that of a control group on amitriptyline. Which of the following tests would be most appropriate?
questions.explanation: The data in this question are not paired data, so options C and E are incorrect as they are used for paired data. The Mann–Whitney U test is used for unpaired data from small samples taken from a non-normally distributed population, which is appropriate for this case. The McNemar test is used for matched analyses and only for actual numbers but not proportions or percentages. Spearman’s correlation is a measure of the relationship between two variables that uses only the ranks of the observations on each. Reference: Lewis GH, Sheringham J, Kalim K, Crayford TJB (2008). Mastering Public Health: A Postgraduate Guide to Examination and Revalidation. London: Royal Society of Medicine Press, pp. 88, 539.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is not true for confounders?

options.text: It can be adjusted for at the analysis stage.
It can be adjusted for at the study design stage.
It may be an intermediate step along the causal chain.
It must be associated with the disease and be independently associated with the exposure under study.
It must predict disease independently of the exposure under study.

correct_answer.text: It may be an intermediate step along the causal chain.

correct_answers.text: It may be an intermediate step along the causal chain.

questions.explanation: Criteria for confounders are that they must be associated with the disease and be independently associated with the exposure under study; they must predict disease independently of the exposure under study and they cannot simply be an intermediate step in the causal chain. Confounders can be countered and controlled for at the design stage or adjusted for at the analysis stage. Reference: Lewis GH, Sheringham J, Kalim K, Crayford TJB (2008). Mastering Public Health: A Postgraduate Guide to Examination and Revalidation. London: Royal Society of Medicine Press, pp. 31–34.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements regarding meta-analysis is incorrect?

options.text: Patricia Forest published the first Forest plot in 1958.
Meta-analysis allows combination of effect sizes from different studies.
Meta-analysis allows comparison of results from studies from different categories.
Meta-analysis is best complemented by meta-regression.
The pooled effect-size is dependent on the variability of source data.

correct_answer.text: Patricia Forest published the first Forest plot in 1958.

correct_answers.text: Patricia Forest published the first Forest plot in 1958.

questions.explanation: There is a misunderstanding that Forest plot is named after a person. Lewis and Clark stated that the origin of Forest refers to the forest of lines produced in the Forest plot. Meta-analysis combines results or effect sizes from different studies and allows comparison of results from different categories by sensitivity analysis. The pooled effect-size is dependent on the variability of source data, known as heterogeneity. Researchers often perform meta-analysis alone without including meta-regression. It is best complemented by meta-regression to identify moderators that explain heterogeneity. Reference: Stanley TD, Jarrell SB (1989). Meta-regression analysis: A quantitative method of literature surveys. J Econ Surv, 19(3): 299–308.

questions.question_text: A 23-year-old man, Samuel, has been recently diagnosed with first-episode psychosis and has been started on a dose of olanzapine. He is having muscular rigidity and fever at the moment. The core trainee is suspecting that he might have neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS). All the following should be suspected as possible differentials with the exception of which one?
questions.explanation: The core signs and symptoms of neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS) include muscle rigidity and fever, as well as altered consciousness, mutism, labile blood pressure, tachycardia, tremor, incontinence and leukocytosis. The differential diagnoses to be considered include central nervous system (CNS) infection, sepsis, serotonin syndrome, lethal catatonia, catatonia, myocardial infarction, heat stroke, malignant hyperthermia and thyroid storm. Heavy metals such as thallium and arsenic are possible differentials but not lead poisoning. Reference: Hall RCW et al. (2006). Neuroleptic malignant syndrome in the elderly: Diagnostic criteria, incidence, risk factors, pathophysiology and treatment. Clin Geriatrics, 14: 39–46.

questions.question_text: Which of the following regarding hyperparathyroidism is false?

options.text: It leads to an increase in serum Mg2+.
Affective disturbance and personality change occur when the serum Ca2+ is 3–4 mmol/L.
Delirium, impaired cognition and psychosis occur when the serum Ca2+ is 4–4.75 mmol/L.
Somnolence and coma occur when the serum Ca2+ is higher than 4–4.75 mmol/L.
One-third of patients with hyperparathyroidism have severe psychiatric problems.

correct_answer.text: It leads to an increase in serum Mg2+.

correct_answers.text: It leads to an increase in serum Mg2+.

questions.explanation: Hyperparathyroidism leads to a reduction in Mg2+, not an increase. Some of the commonly associated neuropsychiatric symptoms include disturbance of mood and drive, delirium (caused by high calcium levels), cognitive impairment and psychosis. Correction of serum calcium usually results in reversal of psychiatric symptoms. Reference: Puri BK, Hall AD, Ho RC (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. Boca Raton, FL: CRC Press, p. 478.

questions.question_text: The purposes for conducting meta-regression include all the following except which of the following?

options.text: To evaluate the evidence obtained from multiple studies involving cost–benefit analysis studies of a health policy across multiple studies.
To examine the impact of different variables on study effect size.
To identify which independent variables are predictors of a dependent variable after adjustment of confounding factors.

correct_answer.text: To identify which independent variables are predictors of a dependent variable after adjustment of confounding factors.

correct_answers.text: To identify which independent variables are predictors of a dependent variable after adjustment of confounding factors.

questions.explanation: In meta-analysis, meta-regression is used to examine the impact of different variables on study effect size, to explain heterogeneity and to identify potential bias. It is also used in policy analysis to evaluate evidence from cost–benefit studies across multiple publications. Option E describes multivariate regression in a single study, not meta-regression. Reference: Stanley TD, Jarrell SB (1989). Meta-regression analysis: A quantitative method of literature surveys. J Econ Surv, 19(3): 299–308.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a predictor for the persistence of hyperkinetic symptoms into adulthood?
questions.explanation: Predictors for persistence of ADHD symptoms into adulthood include family history of ADHD, psychosocial adversity and comorbid conduct, depressive or anxiety disorder. Comorbid language disorders are not a known predictor. Reference: Puri BK, Hall AD, Ho RC (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. Boca Raton, FL: CRC Press, p. 635.

questions.question_text: Which of the following common psychiatric disorders has been known to be associated with the highest heritability?
questions.explanation: The heritability of autistic disorder is over 90%. Recurrence rate in siblings is roughly 3% for narrowly defined autism and 10%–20% for milder variants. Chromosomal loci may involve 2q and 7q. Reference: Puri BK, Hall AD, Ho RC (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. Boca Raton, FL: CRC Press, p. 623.

questions.question_text: An 8-year-old boy demonstrates only speak selectively in certain situations. His mother is very concerned about his condition and wants to know the long-term prognosis of his condition. Based on current evidence, poor prognosis is associated with duration of the condition being longer than?
questions.explanation: Poor prognosis in selective mutism is associated with duration of the condition being longer than 12 months. Reference: Puri BK, Hall AD, Ho RC (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. Boca Raton, FL: CRC Press, p. 642.

questions.question_text: All the following are implicated in the pathophysiology of tic disorder, with the exception of

options.text: Reduction in the levels of noradrenaline
Reduction in choline in the left putamen
Presence of abnormalities in the caudate nucleus

questions.explanation: All listed except increased 5HT3 receptor sensitivity are implicated. Abnormalities in D2 receptor sensitivity, reduction in noradrenaline, reduction in choline in the putamen and caudate nucleus abnormalities have been implicated. Reference: Puri BK, Hall AD, Ho RC (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. Boca Raton, FL: CRC Press, p. 640.

questions.question_text: Pica refers to the persistent eating of non-nutritive substances for at least twice per week for a total minimum duration of 1 month. It usually affects children above the age of
questions.explanation: Based on ICD-10, pica refers to persistent eating of non-nutritive substances at least twice per week for 1 month. The chronological and mental age of the child is usually above 2 years. It is associated with other psychiatric disorders, such as learning disability, psychosis and social deprivation. Reference: Puri BK, Hall AD, Ho RC (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. Boca Raton, FL: CRC Press, p. 642.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a feature of melancholia?
questions.explanation: Melancholia is characterized by anhedonia, excessive guilt, loss of appetite, absence of mood reactivity, psychomotor changes (agitation or retardation), diurnal variation, and terminal insomnia. Mood reactivity is absent. Reference: Puri BK, Hall AD, Ho RC (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. Boca Raton, FL: CRC Press, p. 380.

questions.question_text: A 32-year-old woman has just given birth to her newborn son 3 days ago. Her husband has noted that she has been very tearful, with significant irritability as well as anxiety. Which of the following is a recommended treatment of choice based on NICE guidelines?

options.text: Immediate admission to the inpatient psychiatry unit

questions.explanation: Postnatal blues is a brief psychological disturbance characterized by tearfulness, emotional lability and confusion in the first few days after childbirth, affecting around 50% of women. Reassurance is recommended; no psychotropic medication is required and prognosis is good. Reference: Puri BK, Hall AD, Ho RC (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. Boca Raton, FL: CRC Press, p. 567.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a risk factor for tardive dyskinesia?
questions.explanation: Risk factors for tardive dyskinesia include old age, diffuse brain damage, duration of antipsychotic treatment and affective psychosis. Tardive dyskinesia is more common in females, so male gender is not a risk factor. Reference: Puri BK, Hall AD, Ho RC (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. Boca Raton, FL: CRC Press, p. 201.

questions.question_text: A researcher wants to find out which groups of depressed patients will benefit from taking a new antidepressant recently released on the market. The variables include age, gender, socio-economic status, number of depressive episodes and changes in Hamilton depression scale. Which one of the following analyses is this researcher doing?
questions.explanation: Cluster analysis is a set of methods for constructing classification of an initially unclassified set of data, using the variable values observed in each individual. It involves classifying data into groups (clusters) based on the variable values observed in each individual. Reference: Everitt BS (2006). Medical Statistics from A to Z (2nd edition). Cambridge University Press, p. 48.

questions.question_text: A psychiatrist works in an academic institution with no substance abuse unit. Based on patients with consecutive schizophrenia admitted having no substance abuse, he concludes that there is no real association between schizophrenia and substance abuse. Which bias has this psychiatrist made?
questions.explanation: Berkson’s bias, or hospital admission bias, arises when differential admission rates with respect to a suspected causal factor create a spurious association between disease and exposure. Reference: Everitt BS (2014). Medical Statistics from A to Z (2nd edition). Cambridge University Press, pp. 13, 23, 195.

questions.question_text: A researcher wants to study the prevalence of cannabis-induced psychosis in the community. He recruits patients who are on follow-up in the psychosis clinic. Which type of bias is he experiencing?
questions.explanation: Neyman bias occurs when prevalence studies miss cases that have remitted or died before sampling. By recruiting only clinic follow-up patients, he misses those whose psychosis resolved without referral, underestimating the association. Reference: Lewis GH, Sheringham J, Kalim K, Crayford TJB (2008). Mastering Public Health. Royal Society of Medicine Press, pp. 29–32.

questions.question_text: A 20-year-old woman suffers from anorexia nervosa, and she is 30 weeks pregnant. The obstetrician consults you on the potential problems that may occur during the delivery. The use of which of the following obstetric procedures is known to be increased in pregnant women with anorexia nervosa?
questions.explanation: Pregnant women with active eating disorders have a greater chance for delivery by caesarean section and may develop postpartum depression. Reference: Franko DL et al. (2001). Pregnancy complications and neonatal outcomes in women with eating disorders. Am J Psychiatry, 158: 1461–1466.

questions.question_text: In separation anxiety disorder, the child has anticipatory anxiety of separation. The onset is usually before which one of the following ages?
questions.explanation: In separation anxiety disorder, onset is usually before age 6 years. The child has unrealistic persistent worry about possible harm befalling attachment figures or their loss. Reference: Puri BK, Hall AD, Ho RC (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. Boca Raton, FL: CRC Press, p. 652.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements regarding treatment of ADHD is true?

options.text: Very low birth weight and perinatal insult are risk factors for ADHD.
The half-life of atomoxetine is 15 hours.
Atomoxetine can be given only as second-line agent under all circumstances.
There is evidence to support the use of second-generation antipsychotics to treat hyperactivity in ADHD.
Hyperactivity and epilepsy are mutually exclusive.

correct_answer.text: Very low birth weight and perinatal insult are risk factors for ADHD.

correct_answers.text: Very low birth weight and perinatal insult are risk factors for ADHD.

questions.explanation: Very low birth weight and perinatal insult are risk factors for ADHD. Options B–E are incorrect: atomoxetine half-life ~5 hours; it is first-line for tics; no evidence for second-generation antipsychotics for hyperactivity; hyperactivity can occur with epilepsy. References: Baker P (2004). Basic Child Psychiatry (7th ed.). Blackwell; Taylor D et al. (2009). The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines (10th ed.). Informa Healthcare.

questions.question_text: In which of the following conditions would an electroencephalogram (EEG) demonstrate an increase in slow-wave activity and a reduction in rhythm?
questions.explanation: In CJD, EEG shows increased slow-wave activity and reduced rhythm, progressing to bilateral slow spike-wave discharges with myoclonus. Reference: Puri BK, Hall AD, Ho RC (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. Boca Raton, FL: CRC Press, p. 705.

questions.question_text: Which of the following about the prognosis of Huntington disease is correct?
questions.explanation: Huntington disease has a slowly progressive course with death often occurring 12–16 years after onset. Reference: Puri BK, Hall AD, Ho RC (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. Boca Raton, FL: CRC Press, p. 707.

questions.question_text: A 40-year-old man presents with memory loss and ataxia. The radiologist gives you a call as he has discovered pulvinar signal in his MRI. This MRI finding is associated with which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation: The ‘pulvinar sign’ (high signal in the posterior thalamus) is characteristic of new variant CJD. Reference: Puri BK, Hall AD, Ho RC (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. Boca Raton, FL: CRC Press, p. 701.

questions.question_text: A male adolescent suffers from depression as he has difficulty in coping with changes associated with puberty. He wants to know the average duration of puberty in boys. Your answer is
questions.explanation: Boys enter puberty at an average age of 11 years (range 9–14) and the process lasts about 5–6 years. Reference: Puri BK, Treasaden I (eds) (2010). Psychiatry: An Evidence-Based Text. London: Hodder Arnold, pp. 120–121.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is incorrect?

options.text: Postpartum blues are common and usually have an onset between the third and the fifth days after pregnancy.
The incidence of depression in women in spontaneous abortion and ectopic pregnancy is much higher than that of the general population.
Postpartum psychosis should be regarded as a psychiatric emergency and warrants inpatient hospitalization.
There needs to be careful selection of psychotropic medications as these medications could have potential adverse effects on the infant.
Delusional disorders tend to be worsened in pregnancy.

correct_answer.text: Delusional disorders tend to be worsened in pregnancy.

correct_answers.text: Delusional disorders tend to be worsened in pregnancy.

questions.explanation: Delusional disorders do not tend to be worsened by pregnancy. All other statements are correct regarding perinatal mood disorders. Reference: Puri BK, Treasaden I (eds) (2010). Psychiatry: An Evidence-Based Text. London: Hodder Arnold, pp. 718–721.

questions.question_text: A 45-year-old man presents to the emergency department with clouding of consciousness, hallucinations and marked tremors. The core trainee who examined him noted that he has nystagmus and ophthalmoplegia on examination as well. He went into sustained ventricular fibrillation, which was not responsive to pharmacological management and demised shortly after. If a brain autopsy was performed for him, it is expected that there will be the presence of which of the following changes?

options.text: Petechial hemorrhages in the periaqueductal grey matter
Tau accumulation in the basal ganglia

correct_answer.text: Petechial hemorrhages in the periaqueductal grey matter

correct_answers.text: Petechial hemorrhages in the periaqueductal grey matter

questions.explanation: This clinical picture is Wernicke’s encephalopathy. Autopsy will show petechial hemorrhages in the periaqueductal grey matter and mammillary bodies. Reference: Puri BK, Hall AD, Ho RC (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. Boca Raton, FL: CRC Press, p. 513.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements regarding confounder and bias is incorrect?

options.text: Both confounder and bias can be adjusted for at the analysis stage.
Both confounder and bias can be prevented by having proper study design.
Confounder is a variable that is associated with exposure and outcome, while bias is a systematic error.
Confounder does not lead to false association between exposure and outcome, but bias does.
Confounder is introduced by a third factor independently related to the exposure and outcome, while bias is introduced by the researcher.

correct_answer.text: Confounder does not lead to false association between exposure and outcome, but bias does.

correct_answers.text: Confounder does not lead to false association between exposure and outcome, but bias does.

questions.explanation: Both confounder and bias can lead to false associations between exposure and outcome; neither is immune. Confounder is a variable related to both exposure and outcome, bias is a systematic error introduced by the study conduct. Reference: Lewis GH, Sheringham J, Kalim K, Crayford TJB (2008). Mastering Public Health. Royal Society of Medicine Press, pp. 27–34.

questions.question_text: A new drug, created by a drug company, is being administered to a small group of subjects in an inpatient clinic where they are being monitored constantly. Which phase of the clinical trial is this?
questions.explanation: Phase I trials involve administration of a new drug to a small group of healthy volunteers or patients under close monitoring to assess safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics. Reference: Everitt BS (2006). Medical Statistics from A to Z (2nd ed.). Cambridge University Press, p. 46.

questions.question_text: A new drug, created by a drug company, is being compared with the current standard treatment for a particular condition. Which phase of the clinical trial is this?
questions.explanation: Phase III trials compare a new treatment to standard therapy in large patient groups to confirm efficacy, monitor side effects and collect information for safe use. Reference: Everitt BS (2006). Medical Statistics from A to Z (2nd ed.). Cambridge University Press, p. 46.

questions.question_text: A 28-year-old man has been referred by his GP for help in your mental health service. He has been having obsessions involving non-living objects and is not able to control his sexual desire and, at times, engages in masturbation. Which of the following statements about his behaviour and diagnosis is incorrect?

options.text: This condition is usually more prevalent in males.
Approximately, 50% of men are considered to be homosexuals.
The behaviour is caused by classical conditioning.
This behaviour may be associated with temporal lobe dysfunction.
Treatment usually involves behavioural therapy focusing masturbatory reconditioning and response prevention.

correct_answer.text: Approximately, 50% of men are considered to be homosexuals.

correct_answers.text: Approximately, 50% of men are considered to be homosexuals.

questions.explanation: Fetishism is more common in men, often involving non-living objects or materials. Approximately 20% of men with fetishism are homosexual, not 50%. The behaviour may be caused by classical conditioning and temporal lobe dysfunction. Treatment involves behavioural therapy focusing on masturbatory reconditioning and response prevention. Reference: Puri BK, Hall AD, Ho RC (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. Boca Raton, FL: CRC Press, p. 600.

questions.question_text: Chronic abuse of which of the following substances might result in the development of Goodpasture syndrome?
questions.explanation: Volatile solvents are inhaled for psychoactive effects; chronic use may lead to Goodpasture syndrome, hypokalaemia and optic neuropathy. High doses can cause stupor or death. Reference: Puri BK, Hall AD, Ho RC (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. Boca Raton, FL: CRC Press, p. 550.

questions.question_text: A 55-year-old woman suffered from a heart attack and was resuscitated. She then consults her GP and complains of recurrent nightmares and hypervigilance. She worries that she may suffer from nervous shock, and her GP has referred her for a psychiatric assessment. During the interview, she mentions that she did not have a heart attack. She thinks she developed an anaphylactic shock after an injection and wants to sue the hospital for compensation. Which of the following statements is most likely to be correct?

options.text: There is a high chance that she will be able to return to work after settlement of this case.
She meets the criteria for nervous shock but not PTSD.
You should refer her to see a forensic psychiatrist for a formal medico-legal assessment.

After you write the medical report, she is likely to be unhappy with the fact that you did not support her claim of having nervous shock and will lodge a formal complaint to the chief executive through her lawyer.
She should be referred to see an expert in PTSD for trauma-focused CBT.

correct_answer.text: After you write the medical report, she is likely to be unhappy with the fact that you did not support her claim of having nervous shock and will lodge a formal complaint to the chief executive through her lawyer.

correct_answers.text: After you write the medical report, she is likely to be unhappy with the fact that you did not support her claim of having nervous shock and will lodge a formal complaint to the chief executive through her lawyer.

questions.explanation: This is a case of compensation neurosis. After writing a medical report that does not support her claim, she is likely to be unhappy and may lodge a complaint via her lawyer. Reference: Gunn J, Taylor PJ (1993). Forensic Psychiatry. Butterworth-Heinemann; Puri BK, Treasaden I (eds) (2010). Psychiatry: An Evidence-Based Text. Hodder Arnold, p. 660.

questions.question_text: A 20-year-old woman suffers from anorexia nervosa. Her parents are concerned about her outcome. Which of the following factors indicates a poor prognosis based on the medical literature?
questions.explanation: Later age of onset is a poor prognostic factor in anorexia nervosa. Other poor prognostic factors include long duration of illness, severe weight loss, substance misuse and obsessive-compulsive personality. Reference: Ratnasuriya RH et al. (1991). Anorexia nervosa: Outcome and prognostic factors after 20 years. Br J Psychiatry, 158: 495–502; Puri BK, Treasaden I (eds) (2010). Psychiatry: An Evidence-Based Text. Hodgder Arnold, pp. 687–703, 1063.

questions.question_text: You are a forensic psychiatrist assessing a 33-year-old man convicted of child sexual abuse for his risk of recidivism. What is the likelihood of him being reconvicted of the same crime?
questions.explanation: Fifteen percent of individuals convicted of child sexual abuse are reconvicted of the same crime in England and Wales. Self-report studies suggest rates up to 35%–45%. Reference: Puri BK, Treasaden I (eds) (2010). Psychiatry: An Evidence-Based Text. Hodder Arnold, pp. 767–769, 772, 773, 1242.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a way of reducing bias?

options.text: Blinding of intervention group but not the observer who collects the measurements

correct_answer.text: Blinding of intervention group but not the observer who collects the measurements

correct_answers.text: Blinding of intervention group but not the observer who collects the measurements

questions.explanation: Blinding of the observer who collects measurements or analyses results is necessary to avoid observer and ascertainment bias. Blinding only the intervention group without blinding observers does not reduce bias. Reference: Lewis GH, Sheringham J, Kalim K, Crayford TJB (2008). Mastering Public Health. Royal Society of Medicine Press, pp. 26–31.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a risk factor for development of PTSD?
questions.explanation: Psychopathic traits are a protective factor against PTSD. Risk factors include female gender, low IQ, low socioeconomic status, pre-existing psychiatric disorder, and severity of trauma. Reference: Puri BK, Hall AD, Ho RC (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. Boca Raton, FL: CRC Press, p. 427.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a feature of Ganser syndrome?
questions.explanation: Ganser syndrome is a dissociative disorder characterized by approximate or absurd answers (vorbeireden), clouding of consciousness, somatic conversion, pseudohallucinations and subsequent amnesia. Frank hallucinations are not typical. Reference: Puri BK, Hall AD, Ho RC (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. Boca Raton, FL: CRC Press, p. 434.

questions.question_text: A 70-year-old man was admitted to a general hospital as he felt pain when passing urine. Three days later, he began complaining to his relatives that the ward staff were not treating him well and were poisoning his food. He also saw insects crawling on the wall. The likely diagnosis is
questions.explanation: This patient presents with acute onset of confusion, hallucinations and delusional misidentification in the context of a general medical illness, consistent with delirium. Reference: Puri BK, Treasaden I (eds) (2010). Psychiatry: An Evidence-Based Text. London: Hodder Arnold, p. 880.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not usually found in Addison’s disease?
questions.explanation: Addison’s disease is characterized by low sodium, high potassium, high urea, low glucose and sometimes hypercalcaemia. Low potassium is not found; instead, hyperkalaemia occurs. Reference: Puri BK, Hall AD, Ho RC (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. Boca Raton, FL: CRC Press, p. 477.

questions.question_text: What percentage of patients with anorexia nervosa eventually develop symptoms of bulimia?
questions.explanation: About 50% of restrictive anorexia nervosa patients develop bulimia over time. Anorexia has variable outcomes; adolescent recovery ~80% at 5 years, adult recovery ~50%. Reference: Puri BK, Hall AD, Ho RC (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. Boca Raton, FL: CRC Press, p. 581.

questions.question_text: Which of the following classes of drug has been known to be associated with a high incidence of pulmonary hypertension in the newborn?
questions.explanation: SSRIs, especially when taken in late pregnancy, have been associated with persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn. Withdrawal symptoms such as agitation and irritability may also occur. Reference: Puri BK, Hall AD, Ho RC (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. Boca Raton, FL: CRC Press, p. 561.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a risk factor for suicide in multiple sclerosis?

options.text: Old age at onset of illness

correct_answer.text: Old age at onset of illness

correct_answers.text: Old age at onset of illness

questions.explanation: Young age at onset, male gender, previous depression, social isolation and substance abuse are risk factors. Older age at onset is not. Suicide rates are 7.5 times higher in MS than the general population; 15% of mortality is due to suicide. Reference: Jefferies K (2006). The neuropsychiatry of multiple sclerosis. Adv Psych Treat, 12: 214–220.

questions.question_text: A 55-year-old man presents with coronary artery disease (CAD). His wife asks you what the percentage of patients with CAD who develop depression is. Your answer is
questions.explanation: About 20% of patients with ischemic heart disease have comorbid depression. Major depression is an independent risk factor for CAD and predicts mortality after myocardial infarction. Reference: Puri BK, Hall AD, Ho RC (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. Boca Raton, FL: CRC Press, p. 468.

questions.question_text: A 65-year-old bus driver suffers from post-cerebrovascular accident (CVA) cognitive impairment, and he is referred for assessment of pre-morbid intelligence. A junior psychologist consults you on which test to use. Which of the following would you recommend?
questions.explanation: The NART is a reading test of irregular words; vocabulary is relatively preserved in cognitive decline, so it provides an estimate of premorbid IQ. Reference: Puri BK, Hall AD, Ho RC (2014). Revision Notes in Psychiatry. Boca Raton, FL: CRC Press, p. 96.

questions.question_text: The mortality by suicide in Huntington disease is increased by
questions.explanation: Suicide mortality in Huntington disease is increased by approximately 10-fold compared with the general population. Reference: Schoenfeld M (1984). Increased rate of suicide amongst patients with Huntington’s disease. J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry, 47(12): 1283–1287.

questions.question_text: What is the percentage of patients with Turner syndrome suffering from renal malformations?
questions.explanation: Turner syndrome is associated with renal malformations in 40% of cases.

questions.question_text: What is the percentage of patients with Turner syndrome suffering from hypothyroidism?
questions.explanation: Hypothyroidism occurs in approximately 20% of women with Turner syndrome.

questions.question_text: What is the percentage of patients with Turner syndrome suffering from coarctation of the aorta?
questions.explanation: Coarctation of the aorta is found in about 15% of patients with Turner syndrome.

questions.question_text: What is the percentage of patients with Turner syndrome with a meiotic error that occurred in a paternal meiotic division?
questions.explanation: About 80% of meiotic errors leading to Turner syndrome occur during paternal meiosis.

questions.question_text: Analysis of the effect of several variables upon the time it takes for a specified event to happen.
questions.explanation: Cox regression (proportional hazards model) assesses the impact of multiple variables on time-to-event data.

questions.question_text: Describes the relationship between two numerical variables.
questions.explanation: Simple linear regression describes the linear relationship between a dependent and a single independent numerical variable.

questions.question_text: Analysis of several explanatory variables with one outcome variable.
questions.explanation: Multiple linear regression involves two or more independent variables predicting a continuous outcome variable.

questions.question_text: Subjects are first matched based on some demographic characteristics and then randomly assigned into groups.
questions.explanation: Matched random sampling matches subjects on characteristics, then randomly assigns them to groups.

questions.question_text: Subjects are selected based on an ordering scheme such as odd-numbered houses.
questions.explanation: Systematic sampling uses a sampling frame and selects every nth unit (e.g., odd-numbered houses).

questions.question_text: Involves monitoring of ongoing experiences that vary across and within days in the ward environment.
questions.explanation: Event sampling records experiences or events as they occur naturally, often multiple times per day in situ.

questions.question_text: Subjects are first selected as a group through a random method, and the group will be given the same questionnaire three times in 1 year to seek their view on stigma in mental health.
questions.explanation: Panel sampling selects a random group and follows them longitudinally, surveying them multiple times.

questions.question_text: This is a non-probability sampling and subjects are drawn from the part of the population that is available in a clinical service.
questions.explanation: Convenience sampling draws subjects from the readily available segment of the population.

questions.question_text: Subjects are first identified based on characteristics and are then required to provide names of other potential subjects.
questions.explanation: Snowball sampling asks initial subjects to refer others with the required characteristics.

questions.question_text: Subjects are arranged in areas such as inner-city, suburban and rural areas, and subjects from these areas are selected.
questions.explanation: Cluster sampling selects entire clusters (e.g., geographic areas) and samples within them.

questions.question_text: Name three examples of cortical dementia.
questions.explanation: Cortical dementias include Alzheimer’s dementia, frontal lobe dementia and Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (CJD).

questions.question_text: Name three examples of subcortical dementia.
questions.explanation: Subcortical dementias include HIV-related dementia, Huntington chorea and Parkinson disease dementia.

questions.question_text: Name two examples of mixed cortical and subcortical dementia.
questions.explanation: Mixed dementias include vascular dementia and dementia with Lewy bodies (LBD).

questions.question_text: The percentage of prisoners with epilepsy.
questions.explanation: A meta-analysis found a 1% prevalence of epilepsy among prisoners.

questions.question_text: The percentage of arsonists who are male.
questions.explanation: About 80% of arsonists are male.

questions.question_text: The percentage of psychiatric patients released from medium secure units who re-offend.
questions.explanation: Approximately 50% of patients discharged from medium secure units reoffend within 2 years.

questions.question_text: The percentage heritability of antisocial behaviour in prisoners.
questions.explanation: Heritability of antisocial behaviour in prisoners has been estimated at 45%.
