questions.question_text: The percentage of prisoners who screen positive for adult ADHD.
questions.explanation: About 35% of prisoners screen positive for adult ADHD.

questions.question_text: The percentage of female prisoners with antisocial personality disorder.
questions.explanation: About 20% of female prisoners meet criteria for antisocial personality disorder.

questions.question_text: A rating scale used to screen for dementia.
questions.explanation: The Mini Mental State Examination (MMSE) is a commonly used dementia screening tool.

questions.question_text: An automated computerized battery used for cognitive assessment of dementia.
questions.explanation: The Cambridge Neuropsychological Test Automated Battery (CANTAB) is an automated cognitive assessment for dementia.

questions.question_text: An assessment schedule consisting of a structured clinical interview, a range of objective tests and a structured interview with a relative of the patient with dementia.
questions.explanation: The Cambridge Examination for Mental Disorders of the Elderly (CAMDEX) includes interviews, objective tests (CAMCOG) and a relative interview.

questions.question_text: Based on NICE guidelines, which modality of therapy has been recommended to be offered to individuals with severe PTSD within 3 months of the trauma?
questions.explanation: NICE recommends trauma-focused CBT be offered to individuals with severe PTSD within 3 months of trauma.

questions.question_text: Which of the above modalities of therapy help to stop the symptoms of PTSD?
questions.explanation: Trauma-focused CBT and EMDR help to stop PTSD symptoms by reprocessing traumatic memories.

questions.question_text: Based on NICE guidelines, which medications are likely to be beneficial for PTSD and should be used first?
questions.explanation: Fluoxetine, paroxetine, sertraline and venlafaxine have demonstrated benefit and are recommended first for PTSD.

questions.question_text: Which medications can help to reduce the hyperarousal and intrusive symptoms?
questions.explanation: Carbamazepine and clonidine help reduce hyperarousal and intrusive symptoms in PTSD.

questions.question_text: Which medications can help to reduce and lessen the fear-induced startle response?
questions.explanation: Buspirone may help reduce the fear-induced startle response in PTSD.

questions.question_text: What is the approximate highest prevalence of epilepsy commonly reported in studies of patients with Down syndrome?
questions.explanation: Studies report epilepsy prevalence of 1%–13% in Down syndrome, with a maximum around 10%.

questions.question_text: What is the prevalence of Alzheimer’s disease at the age of 50–59 years in Down syndrome?
questions.explanation: The prevalence of Alzheimer’s disease in Down syndrome at ages 50–59 is approximately 36%–40%.

questions.question_text: What is the prevalence of Alzheimer’s disease at the age of 60–69 years in Down syndrome?
questions.explanation: The prevalence of Alzheimer’s disease in Down syndrome at ages 60–69 is about 55%.

questions.question_text: What is the percentage resulting from translocation of chromosome 21 in Down syndrome?
questions.explanation: About 5% of Down syndrome cases are due to Robertsonian translocations of chromosome 21.

questions.question_text: What is the average life expectancy in Down syndrome?
questions.explanation: Average life expectancy for individuals with Down syndrome is approximately 58–66 years.

questions.question_text: What is the percentage with leukaemia in Down syndrome?
questions.explanation: Around 10% of individuals with Down syndrome develop leukemia.

questions.question_text: What is the percentage with hearing loss in Down syndrome?
questions.explanation: Hearing loss occurs in about 50% of people with Down syndrome.

questions.question_text: What is the percentage with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) in Down syndrome?
questions.explanation: Approximately 2% of individuals with Down syndrome meet criteria for OCD.

questions.question_text: A 45-year-old woman with excessive tiredness, lethargy and constipation likely has which endocrine disorder?
questions.explanation: Hypothyroidism commonly presents with fatigue, lethargy, constipation and may impair job performance.

questions.question_text: A 30-year-old woman with anxiety, facial flushing, tachycardia and weight loss despite good appetite likely has which endocrine disorder?
questions.explanation: Hyperthyroidism presents with anxiety, flushing, tachycardia and weight loss despite good appetite.

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old woman with irregular menses, weight gain, acne and depression likely has which endocrine disorder?
questions.explanation: Cushing syndrome is associated with weight gain, acne, irregular menses and depressive symptoms.

questions.question_text: A 30-year-old woman with weakness, hypotension, hyperpigmentation and memory difficulties likely has which endocrine disorder?
questions.explanation: Addison disease presents with weakness, postural hypotension, hyperpigmentation and cognitive difficulties.

questions.question_text: A 60-year-old woman with polydipsia, polyuria, low urine osmolality and high plasma osmolality likely has which endocrine disorder?
questions.explanation: Diabetes insipidus features excessive thirst, polyuria, low urine osmolality and high plasma osmolality.

questions.question_text: Children and young people with learning disability who have an additional diagnosable psychiatric disorder; approximate percentage?
questions.explanation: About 36% of children and young people with learning disability have a comorbid psychiatric disorder.

questions.question_text: Patients with learning disability developing dementia at the age of 65 years; approximate percentage?
questions.explanation: Approximately 20% of people with learning disability have dementia by age 65, compared with 5.7% of the general population.

questions.question_text: Patients with epilepsy who have mild learning disability; approximate percentage?
questions.explanation: About 7%–15% of individuals with mild learning disability have a lifetime history of epilepsy.

questions.question_text: Children with autism who have learning disability; approximate percentage?
questions.explanation: Approximately 70% of children with autism spectrum disorder have an associated learning disability.

questions.question_text: In the event that an anti-dementia drug patient has asthma, which one of the anti-dementia drugs is contraindicated?
questions.explanation: Donepezil is contraindicated in patients with asthma due to its cholinergic side effects.

questions.question_text: Which of the following side effects are common for anti-dementia medications (nausea, diarrhoea, dizziness, urinary incontinence, parasympathetic stimulation and reduction in heart rate)?
questions.explanation: Cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) commonly cause these cholinergic side effects.

questions.question_text: In this condition, the first symptom is always daytime sleepiness, occurring during adolescence with hypersomnia, sleep attacks and sleep paralysis.
questions.explanation: Narcolepsy typically presents in adolescence with excessive daytime sleepiness, sleep attacks and sleep paralysis.

questions.question_text: This is considered to be the most common breathing-related sleep disorder.
questions.explanation: Obstructive sleep apnoea is the most common breathing-related sleep disorder.

questions.question_text: This is a common sleep condition associated with autoimmune thyroid disorders, iron deficiency and diabetes mellitus.
questions.explanation: Restless leg syndrome is associated with autoimmune thyroid disorders, iron deficiency and diabetes mellitus.

questions.question_text: This is a sleep condition that is common in children and occurs on a frequent basis in 1%–4%.
questions.explanation: Sleep terrors occur in 1%–4% of children and are characterized by sudden extreme fear during non-REM sleep.

questions.question_text: The risk of schizophrenia in his child if his wife also suffers from schizophrenia.
questions.explanation: If both parents have schizophrenia, the risk in offspring is approximately 35%–50%.

questions.question_text: The risk of schizophrenia in his child if his wife does not suffer from schizophrenia.
questions.explanation: If only one parent has schizophrenia, the offspring risk is about 10%–14%.

questions.question_text: The risk of schizophrenia if he adopted a child with DiGeorge syndrome.
questions.explanation: DiGeorge syndrome (22q11 deletion) carries a 20%–24% risk of developing schizophrenia.

questions.question_text: The risk of schizophrenia in his half-siblings.

questions.question_text: The risk of schizophrenia in his younger cousin.
questions.explanation: First cousins share 12.5% of genes; the risk of schizophrenia is approximately 0%–4%.

questions.question_text: The risk of schizophrenia in his nephew or niece.
questions.explanation: A nephew shares about 25% of genes via the sibling route, but empirical risk is similar to cousins (0%–4%).

questions.question_text: The risk of schizophrenia in his biological uncles or aunties.
The percentage of people with schizophrenia who do not continue with antipsychotic after 1 year.
questions.explanation: Approximately 70%–75% of patients with schizophrenia discontinue antipsychotic medication within one year.

questions.question_text: The percentage of people with schizophrenia who smoke.
questions.explanation: About 80%–85% of individuals with schizophrenia are current smokers.

questions.question_text: A crossover study of 30 female depressed patients treated with SSRI and placebo, cytokine levels measured during each phase; which test is appropriate?
questions.explanation: A paired t-test compares means of two related samples (same subjects under SSRI vs placebo) assuming normal distribution of differences.

questions.question_text: Five years later, the same MCI patients have follow-up homocysteine levels (skewed) compared with baseline and dementia status; which test is useful to test hypothesis of changes in levels?
questions.explanation: Wilcoxon rank sum test (a nonparametric paired comparison) is used for skewed paired data when normality is not assumed.

questions.question_text: Baseline low/medium/high homocysteine in MCI vs controls and effect on subsequent dementia; which tests?
questions.explanation: Chi-squared test compares proportions (MCI vs control incidence). Mann–Whitney U test assesses differences in homocysteine rankings between groups.

questions.question_text: A researcher compares quality-of-life (SF-36) scores of depressed patients on TCAs, SSRIs and SNRIs (assumed normally distributed); which test?
questions.explanation: One-way ANOVA compares means of more than two independent groups when data are normally distributed.

questions.question_text: In a postgraduate psychiatric exam with close marking (scores 4–7), chief examiner compares median scores among local, immigrant and refugee doctors; which test?
questions.explanation: Kruskal–Wallis test compares medians of more than two independent groups without assuming normal distribution.

questions.explanation: Lifetime prevalence of substance misuse or dependence in schizophrenia is about 50%.

questions.question_text: The lifetime prevalence of substance misuse or dependence in people with bipolar affective disorder.
